Q: When should an AI application use SSE?
A: Server-Sent Events suit a server-to-browser stream of text or task progress over HTTP. Use a separate request to submit work or cancel a task when bidirectional messaging is unnecessary.
Why: Define a stable event schema and stream the safe projection of run state. SSE is a transport for events, not a durable task engine.
Risk: An open connection does not prove that work is persisted or authorized.
Trade: SSE fits HTTP infrastructure and offers only one-way messaging on that connection.
Try: Compare a chat answer stream with a collaborative voice interaction.
spoken: SSE suits server-to-client events when its browser/HTTP constraints fit. Implement proper event framing, explicit terminal states and durable replay if promised. EventSource reconnection and Last-Event-ID only help when the server honors a valid replay contract. Bound server queues and handle slow readers.

follow_ups.Q: Does EventSource expose automatic application-level backpressure?
follow_ups.A: No. Define bounded server buffering, disconnect/drop policy and replay behavior; do not assume the browser API solves overload.

Q: How is an SSE message framed?
A: An event consists of text fields followed by a blank line. Data may span multiple data lines, which the receiver combines according to SSE rules. Network chunks do not align with event boundaries.
Why: Decode UTF-8 incrementally, accumulate lines, and dispatch only at the event delimiter. Normalize supported line endings and impose limits.
Risk: Parsing each received chunk as JSON fails when characters or messages split across chunks.
Trade: Correct incremental parsing adds state and avoids intermittent corruption.
Try: Split a Unicode event at every byte boundary and verify equivalent decoding.

Q: How should EventSource and fetch streaming be compared?
A: Browser EventSource handles an SSE GET connection and reconnection behavior. Fetch streaming gives control over methods, headers, and request bodies but requires application parsing and retry logic.
Why: Choose based on authentication, request semantics, and resume requirements. Do not assume EventSource accepts arbitrary authorization headers.
Risk: Putting bearer tokens in query parameters can expose them in logs and history.
Trade: Fetch offers flexibility while EventSource supplies useful protocol behavior.
Try: Design a cookie-authenticated EventSource flow and a header-authenticated fetch flow.

Q: What should a public AI event schema contain?
A: Include schema version, task ID, ordered sequence, event type, and typed payload. Distinguish text deltas, tool activity, final results, recoverable notices, and terminal errors.
Why: Convert provider events through an adapter. The UI should reduce these events into explicit states rather than concatenate every payload into answer text.
Risk: Provider-internal messages can leak private arguments or confuse partial output with completion.
Trade: Stable schemas add adapter maintenance and protect the UI from provider churn.
Try: Document how a tool error changes state differently from an answer delta.

Q: How should reconnection and replay work?
A: Give events durable sequence IDs and define a retention window. Resume from the last acknowledged or processed event, and deduplicate repeated sequence numbers.
Why: If replay history expired, return a snapshot or a clear resume failure. Revalidate ownership on every connection.
Risk: Reconnecting without a replay contract can lose events or duplicate displayed text.
Trade: Durable event storage adds cost and enables recovery.
Try: Disconnect after event seven and resume without repeating the final business operation.

Q: How do heartbeats and proxy buffering affect streams?
A: Intermediaries may buffer output or close idle connections. Heartbeats can keep an otherwise idle stream active, but infrastructure behavior must be measured.
Why: Use appropriate content type and cache policy, disable buffering where supported, and send bounded periodic comments. Check actual arrival times through the production proxy.
Risk: Application flushes alone do not establish that the browser receives each event promptly.
Trade: Frequent heartbeats consume connections and bandwidth.
Try: Record server-send and browser-receive timestamps behind your actual ingress.

Q: How should cancellation work with SSE?
A: Closing a stream should stop unnecessary generation according to product policy, while durable tasks may continue independently. Expose a task cancellation endpoint for explicit control.
Why: Propagate cancellation to providers when supported and record the final task state. Preserve committed operation IDs for later lookup.
Risk: A disconnected stream does not prove that external effects were cancelled.
Trade: Separating task and stream lifetimes adds complexity and enables background completion.
Try: Close the stream during a pending tool call and inspect the authoritative task status.

A: Bound producer-to-writer queues and prevent slow clients from retaining unlimited memory. Decide which progress events can be coalesced and which terminal events must be retained.
Why: Await writable capacity where the framework supports it, monitor queue depth, and disconnect consumers that cannot keep up under the contract.
Risk: Dropping arbitrary text deltas corrupts the answer.
Trade: Strong limits may disconnect slow clients and protect the server.
Try: Simulate a client reading one event per second while the producer emits many more.

Q: What should completion mean in an SSE stream?
A: A completion event should identify the persisted result or authoritative final task state. A finished model token sequence is not necessarily a completed application operation.
Why: Persist the final record before emitting completion and support owner-scoped result retrieval after disconnect.
Risk: A crash after sending done but before commit creates a false success.
Trade: Persist-before-complete adds final latency and strengthens recovery.
Try: Crash at the completion boundary and verify the UI can recover from the result endpoint.

A: Test UTF-8 boundaries, multiline data, line endings, comments, empty data, malformed payloads, replay, authorization, disconnects, and slow consumers. Test through the real proxy as well as in process.
Why: Keep transport decoding separate from JSON schema validation and UI reduction. Assert both event order and terminal state.
Risk: A happy-path mock stream misses buffering and network fragmentation.
Trade: Real transport tests cost more and catch difficult intermittent failures.
Try: Build a replay fixture containing a duplicate event and an expired resume token.
